title: Knowledge Must Follow the Work
description: I am starting VALESKA as software so the knowledge system can show the work the way a value-stream map shows it — not the way a departmental filing system shows it.
body:
I am starting VALESKA as a working repository because I need the knowledge system to show the same thing a value-stream map shows: how the work actually runs. A document system that files by department or by subject cannot do that. It stores the memory of the work in a shape the work itself does not have. That is the split I am building this software to close.

I first saw the split in 2004, at Northrop Grumman. Value-stream thinking made manufacturing visible. The map showed the connected activities that turn an input into something a customer can use — and it showed the handoffs, the waits, the rework, and who owned each step. The enterprise content system, sitting next to that map, was organized in a completely different way. Documents lived in departmental trees, topical taxonomies, or the folder habits people already had. Those structures are easy to recognize. They do not describe how the organization produces value. So the plant could be told to think Lean on the floor while its memory of methods, decisions, and evidence was still filed as if the silos were the truth.

That is how you get islands of success. A process works in one cell. It cannot spread, because the next cell cannot find the method, the decision, or the evidence in the shape of the stream. They can find a department, or a topic. They cannot walk the work. We are taught to think in functions, and Lean asks the enterprise to break those silos. It never fails that the knowledge system leaves them standing. A document is not a topic. It is an artifact of work: an input, a decision, a handoff, a control, a method, or evidence of an outcome. Its place has to say what it is for, who uses it, and what comes before and after it. That was the beginning of the Value Stream Knowledge Architecture.

The same argument, in something that can be built

I presented that argument at Northrop as a way to connect value-stream analysis with enterprise content management. It asked people to change how they thought about information, ownership, and structure. It was too radical to become the operating model. I did not drop it. I kept writing it. The early VSKA papers are the same claim in older tools: align the knowledge system to the process already in place, and the artifact falls into place. Most people browse; they do not search. Repeatable process structure is the road they already know how to walk. Permissions should follow that same hierarchy, one to one, so security is simpler and therefore more secure. Topical trees are hard to lock down. Functional trees fight Lean. No system I had seen was structured on process.

I wrote Architexturizer in C++ so the argument would not remain a diagram. The name was the job: give the architecture enough structure that it could be constructed, populated, and used. In Livelink that meant building and loading a process workspace instead of drawing folders by hand. This repository is that job again, in software we can run. I am not inventing the idea today. I am taking the process, the vocabulary, and the security model I already wrote and putting them where they can be executed.

What has to be true of the software

If the document's place is its place in the work, then I cannot start by moving the files. The files are already where the work is. I have to find them there, give each one an identity, attach it to a shared process vocabulary instead of a private folder dialect, and make it findable without dropping the access rules that already belong to it. APQC is that shared vocabulary. A scanner, metadata, embeddings, and PostgreSQL with pgvector are how the identity and the finding are held. None of those pieces is the point. The point is that a useful result is still a document connected to its source, its owner, its location, and its permissions — a record of work, not a hit that has forgotten where it came from.

Alfresco is the planned home for browsing, because people will keep walking the systems they already have. VALESKA has to make that landscape follow the work. It should not demand a new landscape. The question hanging over this first commit is the same split I saw in 2004, now asked of software: can a process taxonomy, applied to files we do not move, actually help someone find the work without breaking the permission model those files already have? I have not run that test on a real collection. Today I have a design I can execute, and a history I am no longer willing to leave on paper.

Historical basis: VALESKA initial repository commit be8a50a, August 8, 2025; VALESKA_SDD.md. The Northrop and Architexturizer material is my firsthand account, with early VSKA documents retained as supporting artifacts.
